hair.title: Why Korea Treats the Scalp as Skin
hair.h1: Scalp-first haircare: why Korea treats the scalp as skin
hair.qa: Korean haircare starts at the scalp because the scalp is skin — the same barrier, the same oil glands, the same tendency to get irritated — and Korean brands build their routines around that fact. In practice it means cleansing, hydrating, soothing and occasionally exfoliating the scalp much as you would the face, then handling the lengths as a separate job. It is a sensible organising idea rather than a promise of thicker hair.

sections.body: The scalp is skin. It has the same barrier, the same nerve endings and the densest population of sebaceous glands on the body, and it gets stripped, irritated and dehydrated by the same things — harsh surfactants, hot water, dye, friction, sun. Korea's haircare aisle takes that literally: 두피 (dupi, scalp) products are cleansed, toned, soothed and occasionally exfoliated in a sequence that would look familiar on a bathroom shelf for the face. The hair itself is treated as a separate, non-living material with entirely different needs.

sections.h: How it changes the product shelf
sections.body: Walk a Korean haircare aisle and the sorting logic differs from most Western shops. Shampoos are grouped by scalp condition — oily, dry, sensitive, flaking — rather than by hair type, and alongside them sit scalp tonics, scalp ampoules, scalp scalers and scalp packs with no obvious counterpart abroad. Masks, oils and leave-ins occupy their own section for the lengths. The practical effect is that a Korean routine often has you buying two things: one for the skin under the hair, one for the hair itself.

A comfortable scalp is worth having on its own terms — less itch, less flaking, less of the greasy feeling that pushes people into daily aggressive washing. There is also a cosmetic payoff at the root: hair that is not weighed down by sebum and residue sits with more lift, which reads as fullness in a mirror and in photographs. Those are real, repeatable results. They are also modest ones, and they concern how the scalp feels and how hair looks rather than how much hair you have.

The trouble starts when 'the scalp is skin' is extended into an implied promise that a cosmetic acting on skin can act on follicle biology. It cannot, and the leap from a cooling tonic to visible regrowth is marketing, not evidence. The second failure mode is enthusiasm: scalp exfoliation borrowed wholesale from facial routines, done twice weekly with a stiff brush, leaves plenty of people with a tighter, more irritated scalp than they started with. If hair is genuinely thinning, that is a dermatologist's question, not a shelf's.

hair.title: Korean Scalp Tonics: What They Can and Cannot Do
hair.h1: Korean scalp tonics: an honest account of what they do
hair.qa: A Korean scalp tonic is a lightweight liquid applied to the scalp after washing to leave it feeling clean, cool and comfortable and to reduce the appearance of flaking and greasiness between washes. It can genuinely change how a scalp feels and how hair sits at the root. It cannot regrow hair, and any tonic implying otherwise is overreaching.

sections.h: What is actually in the bottle
sections.body: Most Korean scalp tonics are a thin water-and-alcohol base carrying a short list of familiar actives: menthol for the cold hit, salicylic acid at cosmetic strength to loosen flakes, panthenol and niacinamide for feel, plus the botanicals Korea leans on — heartleaf (어성초, eoseongcho), ginseng, green tea, sometimes caffeine. The alcohol is doing real work as a carrier and evaporation aid, which is why tonics dry down in seconds instead of sitting greasily on the roots. Some newer formulas drop it, and those feel noticeably heavier.

Sensory effects and appearance. A tonic can leave the scalp feeling clean and cool for hours, cut the itch that makes people scratch and worsen flaking, and reduce the greasy look at the roots on the second day after washing. Because the roots stay lighter, hair holds more lift. None of this is trivial — comfort is the main reason anyone sticks with a routine — but it is worth naming for what it is: a change in how the scalp feels and how hair looks, not a change to the follicle.

Caffeine, topically applied biotin and most of the botanical extract list are supported by thin evidence — laboratory work, small studies, or nothing published at all. Korean packaging sometimes carries a legally defined claim about relieving hair-loss symptoms, which is a regulated cosmetic phrase with a narrow meaning and not the same as a claim to grow hair. Anything promising visible density in weeks is over-claiming. If evidence of that strength existed, the product would be regulated as a medicine and sold accordingly.

Apply to the scalp, not the hair. Part in sections, dispense along each parting, and massage for half a minute with fingertips rather than nails. Damp or dry both work; it is not rinsed out. Daily use suits most people, though sensitive or already-flaking scalps often do better with an alcohol-free formula, since a stinging scalp is not a sign anything is working. Patch-test behind the ear if fragrance or menthol tends to bother you, and give any tonic several weeks before deciding.

hair.title: Hair Loss in Korea: Why It's Mainstream Beauty Talk
hair.h1: 탈모 (talmo): why hair loss is mainstream beauty talk in Korea
hair.qa: Hair loss — 탈모 (talmo) — is discussed openly in Korea and has its own aisle, its own regulated cosmetic category and a large clinic industry behind it. Korean law permits certain cosmetics to claim they help relieve the symptoms of hair loss, which is a cosmetic claim rather than a medical one. Anything that genuinely acts on hair growth is a medicine, and that conversation belongs with a doctor.

sections.body: Hair loss carries less stigma as a topic in Korea than in many places. Dermatology clinics are numerous and relatively accessible, scalp-care aisles are large and unembarrassed, and 탈모 turns up in ordinary conversation and advertising rather than being whispered about. Younger customers, women included, buy scalp care preventively rather than after a crisis. Whether that reflects a genuinely different pattern of hair loss or simply a culture that watches appearance closely and acts early is not something anyone should claim to know precisely.

Korea has a legal category called 기능성화장품 (functional cosmetics), and one of its permitted purposes is helping to relieve the symptoms of hair loss. Products in it are built around a short notified ingredient list — including things such as dexpanthenol, biotin and l-menthol — and must carry the approved wording rather than freestyle claims. That is genuinely useful for shoppers, because the sentence on the bottle has a defined meaning. It remains a cosmetic claim about symptoms and appearance, sitting well below what a prescribed medicine does.

sections.h: What a shampoo can and cannot do
sections.body: A good scalp shampoo removes sebum and residue, calms itching, and reduces the flaking that makes a scalp look and feel inflamed. If hair has been breaking near the root or shedding because the scalp was in poor condition, improving that condition can reduce what you see in the drain. What it does not do is alter the pattern of androgenetic hair loss, which is driven by hormones and inheritance and does not respond to a cleanser, however expensive the bottle or evocative the herb list.

Sudden shedding, patchy bald spots, a sore or scaly scalp, hair loss alongside fatigue or weight change, or anything progressing quickly should go to a dermatologist rather than into a shopping basket. Effective options exist, they are medicines, and choosing between them depends on your pattern, sex, age and health — which is exactly why this page will not recommend one. Korean clinics handle this routinely and a consultation is inexpensive by international standards. Cosmetic scalp care sits alongside that, not instead of it.

hair.title: The Korean Setting Perm, Explained
hair.h1: 셋팅펌 (setting perm): the Korean salon curl, explained
hair.qa: A setting perm — 셋팅펌 — is a heat perm: the hair is chemically softened, wound onto heated rods and set, producing loose, bouncy curls that read best when the hair is dry and styled. It is the Korean salon default for soft volume rather than tight curl. It is also a chemical process, so the current condition of your hair matters more than the photo you bring in.

sections.body: Korean salons split perms into 열펌 (yeolpeom, heat perm) and the older cold perm. A cold perm is chemistry alone, and its curl is springiest when the hair is wet, relaxing as it dries. A heat perm — the setting perm and its temperature-controlled cousin the digital perm, 디지털펌 — uses heated rods so the curl looks its best on dry, blow-dried hair. That difference explains why so many Korean styles are loose and glossy rather than tightly coiled: they were designed to be seen dry.

The stylist assesses porosity and previous chemical work, then applies a reducing lotion that softens the internal bonds. Hair is rinsed, wound onto heated rods, held while the heat sets the new shape, then neutralised so the bonds reform. It takes the better part of an afternoon, most of it sitting still. Rod size and winding angle decide almost everything about the result, which is why the consultation matters more than the reference image — bring several, and be specific about where you want the volume to sit.

Salons commonly ask you not to wash for a day or two while the new shape settles, and to avoid tying, clipping or sleeping on the curl in a way that flattens it. After that, a gentle shampoo, a mask on the ends every few washes and a leave-in cream or light oil applied while damp will keep the curl defined. Rough towel-drying and daily hot tools undo the look faster than anything else. Air-drying or a diffuser gives the soft, dry-set finish the perm was cut for.

A perm is chemistry performed on a material that does not renew itself. Heavily bleached, very fine or previously straightened hair is a poor candidate, and a good stylist will strand-test or decline. Results vary considerably with thickness and density — the same rods do not give the same curl on everyone. The regrowth line becomes visible after a few months, which means committing to touch-ups or growing it out. If your hair is already fragile, say so directly rather than hoping the appointment goes well.

hair.title: Magic Straight Perm: Korea's Straightening Ritual
hair.h1: 매직 (magic) straight perm: what Korean salons actually do
hair.qa: A magic straight perm softens the hair's internal bonds with a reducing agent, presses the hair flat with a straightening iron, then re-sets the bonds so the hair stays straight until it grows out. It is a structural change rather than a blow-dry, which is why it lasts and why it is demanding on the hair. 볼륨매직 is the variant that keeps lift at the roots instead of pressing everything flat.

sections.body: 매직 (maejik) straightening works in three stages: a reducing agent softens the bonds inside the strand, a straightening iron presses the hair flat while it is in that softened state, and a neutraliser fixes the new shape. The change is permanent for the hair that has been treated — it does not wash out and does not revert in humidity, which is the entire appeal. It also means the only way back is growing it out, so the decision deserves more thought than a styling choice.

Pressing every strand flat from root to tip produces a helmet effect nobody asks for, so Korean salons developed 볼륨매직 (volume magic): the roots keep body while the lengths are straightened. Some clients pair straightened mid-lengths with a setting perm on the ends for a soft curve. If you have fine hair and a tendency to flat roots, raise it at the consultation — whether you get volume magic or a straight magic is decided before any chemistry touches your head, and cannot be adjusted afterwards.

Reduction chemistry plus sustained iron heat is one of the harder things you can do to a strand. Bleached, highlighted or previously permed hair is often unsuitable, and a stylist who refuses or insists on a strand test is doing you a favour. Afterwards the hair is more porous and less forgiving of further heat. Plan chemical services in a deliberate order, with gaps between them, and disclose everything done to your hair over the past year, box colour and home toners included.

For the first day or two, keep the hair loose and straight — no tight ponytails, no clips, no tucking behind the ears, since a kink set into freshly treated hair can persist. Salons usually specify when you may wash. After that it is unglamorous maintenance: a mild, low-sulfate shampoo, a conditioning mask regularly, heat protectant on the rare occasions you use tools, and a trim schedule for the ends. The straightness needs no effort; keeping the hair glossy rather than flat does.

hair.title: Protein vs Moisture Balance in Korean Haircare
hair.h1: Protein and moisture: a useful heuristic, loosely evidenced
hair.qa: Protein and moisture balance is the idea that damaged hair needs hydrolysed proteins to feel stronger and humectants and oils to stay flexible, and that too much of either leaves hair brittle or limp. As a practical heuristic it earns its keep. As science it is loose — 'protein overload' is a community concept rather than a defined clinical one, and several other problems produce identical symptoms.

sections.body: Hydrolysed proteins — keratin, wheat, silk, rice, soy — are fragments small enough to adsorb onto the hair surface and, in part, into the outer layers. They fill microscopic gaps in a roughened cuticle, temporarily stiffen the strand and measurably reduce the force needed to comb through wet hair. That is a genuine, testable cosmetic effect. It is also temporary: the deposit washes off over subsequent shampoos, which is why protein products are a repeated habit rather than a one-off fix and why nothing is permanently altered.

Hair does not drink water in any useful sense; products simply hold a little water in and keep the surface slippery. Humectants such as glycerin and panthenol, oils and fatty alcohols, and cationic conditioning agents like behentrimonium chloride all contribute — the last of these binds to damaged, negatively charged spots on the cuticle and does most of the work people describe as softness. Flexible hair breaks less when combed, and less mechanical breakage is the practical benefit hiding behind the vocabulary.

The folk diagnosis runs like this: hair that feels stiff, straw-like and snaps dry has had too much protein, while hair that is limp, gummy and holds no shape has had too much conditioning. Both descriptions are recognisable and both are non-specific. Buildup, hard water, heat damage and a bad haircut produce the same complaints. Before rebalancing anything, try a clarifying wash and see what remains — a surprising number of protein-overload diagnoses turn out to be residue. Treat the framework as a hypothesis, not a result.

sections.h: How the Korean shelf handles it
sections.body: Korean damaged-hair lines — look for 손상모 (sonsangmo, damaged hair) — usually blend both approaches into a single product rather than making you alternate. Ampoules and masks tend to be protein-forward, everyday conditioners emollient-forward, and salon treatments layer several steps with heat. A workable routine is a conditioning mask most washes, a protein-containing ampoule now and then, and honest attention to what changes. If nothing changes either way, the limiting factor is probably heat, bleach or friction, and no bottle addresses those.

hair.title: Scalp Sunscreen: The Step Almost Everyone Skips
hair.h1: Scalp sun protection: the parting line nobody covers
hair.qa: The scalp burns like any other skin, and the parting and hairline are the areas most exposed and least protected. A brimmed hat is the most reliable answer; scalp mists, sticks and powders help but are almost impossible to apply at anything like the amount their SPF was tested at. Korean brands make good scalp SPF mists, and they are worth owning with realistic expectations.

sections.body: Sunscreen stops at the hairline for almost everyone, and a parting is bare skin pointed directly at the sky. Scalp sunburn is common in people with short hair, thinning hair or a habitual centre part, and sun exposure accumulates there unnoticed because you cannot see it in a mirror. Hair provides some cover, but a parting provides none, and a high ponytail exposes a strip of skin most people never think about until it is pink and sore that evening.

sections.h: What Korean scalp SPF looks like
sections.body: Korean brands sell scalp sun protection mostly as fine mists and sprays applied along the parting, sometimes as sticks, occasionally as tinted powders that double as root-shadow makeup. The formulas are built not to leave hair greasy, crunchy or visibly white, which is why they exist as a separate category rather than someone simply telling you to smear facial sunscreen into your roots. They are pleasant, they take five seconds, and for a commute or a short walk they are a sensible answer.

Sun protection factors are measured at an application density almost nobody achieves, and a spray aimed at a parting through hair achieves far less than that. Treat any scalp SPF as partial cover rather than as the number on the bottle, and remember that reapplication is more awkward still. For a beach day, a long hike or midday in summer, a brimmed hat or a UPF cap does more than any mist. Moving your parting from time to time also spreads the exposure around.

Ultraviolet light degrades hair proteins and pigment as well as skin. The results are familiar enough — colour fading and drifting warm, a rougher feel through the ends, more tangling after a summer of sea and sun. Leave-in products with UV filters or absorbing ingredients help modestly; they are not sunscreen for your head and do nothing for the scalp beneath. For hair, physical cover and rinsing chlorine and salt out promptly do more than most bottles marketed for the purpose.

hair.title: How Koreans Actually Use Hair Oil
hair.h1: Hair oil, the Korean way: less than you think, lower than you think
hair.qa: Korean hair-oil use is deliberately restrained: a few drops warmed between the palms and pressed through the mid-lengths and ends, never the scalp, usually on damp hair after washing and again in tiny amounts on dry hair for shine. Camellia — 동백 (dongbaek) — is the heritage oil behind the habit. Oil coats and smooths the hair; it does not feed it.

sections.body: 동백 (dongbaek) is the camellia, and camellia seed oil is Korea's heritage hair oil, historically smoothed onto long hair to dress it and keep it glossy. It is high in oleic acid, which makes it feel light and sink in quickly rather than sitting on the surface like a heavier oil. Camellia groves in the warm south of the country are still a seasonal tourist draw, and the oil remains on sale — now more often blended into modern serums than pressed and used neat.

Oiling before shampooing serves a different purpose from oiling after. A pre-wash oil limits how much water the hair takes up, and repeated swelling and re-drying is part of what roughens a cuticle over time. Coconut oil has the best evidence here, since its fatty acids penetrate the strand and reduce protein loss during washing; camellia, argan and the rest are far less studied and mostly act as surface conditioning. Applied after washing, any of them sit on the outside, cutting friction and adding shine.

Two or three drops for fine hair, a little more for thick or long — warmed between the palms, pressed into the mid-lengths and ends, with whatever remains smoothed over the surface. Nothing at the roots unless you are deliberately doing a pre-wash treatment. Damp hair takes oil more evenly than dry, and a second pinpoint application on dry ends is how the glossy Korean finish is usually achieved. Too much reads greasy in any light and cannot be corrected without washing again.

Oil does not nourish hair. Hair is not living tissue and has no route to take up nutrition, so ingredient lists boasting vitamins are decorative. What oil does is coat the strand, reduce friction between hairs, discourage water from moving in and out — which is most of what frizz control means — and reflect light. All real, all cosmetic, all gone at the next wash. Split ends stay split; only scissors deal with those. Judged as a finishing product, hair oil is one of the better things on the shelf.

hair.title: Dandruff vs Dry Scalp: How to Tell the Difference
hair.h1: Dandruff or dry scalp? The distinction that changes what you buy
hair.qa: Dandruff — 비듬 (bideum) — usually comes with an oily scalp, larger yellowish flakes and persistent itch, and is associated with a yeast that lives on everyone's skin. A dry scalp sheds small, fine, white flakes and normally comes with dry skin elsewhere. They call for opposite products, which is why the wrong shampoo so often makes things worse. Persistent redness, thick scale or soreness deserves a doctor.

sections.body: Dandruff is generally associated with Malassezia, a yeast present on everyone's scalp, and with the inflammatory response some people mount to it in the presence of sebum. Its flakes tend to be larger, oilier and yellowish, with itch and often a background of redness. A dry scalp is dehydration and barrier disruption: small, fine, white flakes, a tight feeling, and usually dry skin elsewhere on the body. The scalp is oily in one case and not in the other, which is the fastest thing to check.

Dandruff responds to antifungal and anti-flaking actives — zinc pyrithione, piroctone olamine, ketoconazole, selenium sulfide, with salicylic acid to loosen scale — used consistently and left on for a minute or two before rinsing. A dry scalp wants the reverse: less frequent, gentler washing, a low-sulfate cleanser and leave-on hydration with panthenol, glycerin or ceramides. Using a medicated anti-dandruff shampoo on a scalp that is merely dry reliably makes it worse, and is the most common self-inflicted scalp problem there is.

Anti-dandruff actives in Korea often place a shampoo in the 의약외품 (uiyagoepum, quasi-drug) category, which is printed on the bottle and is a useful signal that a real active is present at a working level. Products aimed at a dry, tight scalp are instead labelled with 진정 (jinjeong, calming) and 보습 (boseup, moisturising) and sit in the ordinary cosmetics category. Reading those few words saves a great deal of guesswork in an aisle where every bottle looks much like the next.

Persistent redness, thick adherent scale, weeping, soreness, hair loss in the affected patches, or flaking that ignores months of the correct products is not a shopping problem. Seborrhoeic dermatitis, scalp psoriasis and contact reactions to hair dye all present as 'dandruff that will not go away' and are managed differently by a clinician. A dermatologist can distinguish them in a short appointment, and in Korea that appointment is easy to get. Do not spend a year cycling through shampoos to avoid it.

hair.title: Hard Water and Hair: What Actually Changes
hair.h1: Hard water and hair: a real effect with oversold solutions
hair.qa: Hard water leaves calcium and magnesium deposits on hair, which makes it feel rough, look duller and lather poorly, and can shift the tone of colour-treated hair. The effect is real, gradual, and largely reversible with a chelating wash. Korean tap water is generally on the softer side, which is one small reason visitors often say their hair behaves better in Seoul than at home.

sections.h: What hardness does to a strand
sections.body: Hard water carries dissolved calcium and magnesium. Hair has a negatively charged surface, particularly where the cuticle is already damaged, so those positive ions bind and accumulate wash after wash. Laboratory work on hair exposed to hard water reports a rougher surface and reduced strength, and the everyday version is familiar: hair that feels coarse, looks dull, tangles more and refuses to lather. Colour-treated hair shows it first, since mineral deposits shift tone and mineral-loaded hair holds and loses pigment unevenly.

sections.h: It is harder to be certain than people think
sections.body: Almost every complaint attributed to hard water is also produced by product buildup, heat damage, chlorine or plain over-conditioning, and none of them can be told apart in a mirror. The cheapest test is a chelating or clarifying wash: if hair feels markedly better after one or two, minerals and residue were part of the story. If nothing changes, the cause lies elsewhere and buying water hardware will not fix it. Diagnose before you spend, because the hardware is not cheap.

Chelating shampoos containing EDTA, citric acid or phytic acid bind minerals and rinse them away, and used every week or two they stop deposits building. They are drying, so pair them with a conditioning mask. Shower filters are oversold: most reduce chlorine, which is worth something, but genuine softening requires ion exchange, and a small in-line cartridge does not do that. A final rinse with distilled water is chemistry that works and logistics that do not, unless you limit it to the ends.

Tap water across most of Korea is on the softer side, and visitors from hard-water regions often notice hair that lathers more easily and feels smoother within a few days of arriving. It is one plausible reason people credit Korean products with results they may partly owe to the plumbing. Humidity, diet, sleep and an entirely new routine all change at once on a trip, so attribute cautiously — and re-test a product at home before restocking a whole shelf of it.

hair.title: Korean Hair Masks and the Salon Clinic Habit
hair.h1: 헤어팩 and 클리닉: how Korea looks after the lengths
hair.qa: Korean haircare looks after the lengths with masks — 헤어팩 (heeopaek) — and with in-salon 클리닉 (clinic) treatments, which are stronger, heat-assisted versions of the same idea. Both work by depositing conditioning agents and proteins that smooth the cuticle and make hair far easier to comb. The effects are real, cosmetic and temporary; this is maintenance, not restoration.

sections.body: A hair mask is a concentrated conditioner: cationic surfactants such as behentrimonium chloride, fatty alcohols, silicones or their newer substitutes, hydrolysed proteins and oils. The cationic ingredients carry a positive charge and are drawn to the damaged, negatively charged parts of the cuticle, so conditioning lands preferentially where the hair is worst. The result is a smoother surface, far less force needed to comb, more shine and less breakage on the way through. It coats the strand; it does not rebuild it.

Korean salons sell multi-step treatments called 클리닉 (keullinik, clinic) — several products applied in sequence, driven in with steam or a heat cap, then sealed with a cool rinse. The effect is a stronger, longer-lasting version of what a home mask does, typically fading over several washes. The same word appears on retail packaging where nothing clinical is involved. Booked before a wedding or a photoshoot, they earn their price. Booked as a fix for over-bleached hair, they disappoint.

sections.h: Getting more out of a home mask
sections.body: Squeeze the hair out properly first, because a mask applied to soaking hair is a diluted mask. Work it through the mid-lengths and ends, skip the roots, and comb it through so it lands evenly — that matters more than which brand you bought. Mild warmth from a shower cap helps a little. Give it the time on the label; leaving it overnight adds almost nothing, since deposition plateaus quickly. Rinse cooler, and judge the result the next day when the hair is dry.

Masks and bond-building products are sold with molecular diagrams implying the strand is being reconstructed from the inside. Deposition onto a damaged cuticle is real and measurable; returning a bleached strand to its original state is not, and no cosmetic manages it. The honest test is whether your hair combs more easily, breaks less and still looks good a week later — not how it feels in the ten minutes after rinsing, when almost every conditioner in existence performs beautifully.

hair.title: Colour-Treated Hair: The Korean Aftercare Approach
hair.h1: Colour-treated hair: what Korean aftercare actually addresses
hair.qa: Colour, and especially bleach, lifts the cuticle and strips part of the hair's surface lipid layer, leaving it more porous, rougher and quicker to lose tone. Korean aftercare concentrates on gentle mildly acidic washing, cationic conditioning, protein-containing masks and colour-depositing treatments that slow the fade. None of it returns the strand to its pre-bleach state — the honest goal is manageable, glossy-looking hair between salon visits.

sections.body: Oxidative colour and bleach work by opening the cuticle and altering the pigment inside. In the process the strand loses part of its outer lipid layer, 18-MEA, the coating that makes healthy hair water-repellent and slippery. Without it, hair becomes porous and water-loving: it tangles, absorbs product unevenly, dries slowly, stretches more when wet and loses tone faster. Every later complaint about colour-treated hair follows from that single change, which is why bleached hair behaves differently rather than simply looking different.

sections.h: Why ash tones fade so fast
sections.body: 애쉬 (aesyu, ash) and cool brown tones are a Korean salon signature and the hardest colours to keep. Cool pigments are small and wash out first, the warmth underneath is exposed as they go, and reaching the tone required more lifting to begin with. Colour-depositing home treatments — 컬러트리트먼트 — top the pigment back up between visits and slow the drift far more effectively than any shampoo labelled colour-protecting. Wash less often, wash cooler, and accept that the salon photo is a first-week photo.

sections.h: The aftercare that earns its place
sections.body: A mild, low-sulfate shampoo, ideally 약산성 (yaksanseong, mildly acidic), used on the scalp rather than scrubbed through the lengths. A conditioning mask most washes. A leave-in with slip and some heat protection, since porous hair suffers disproportionately from tools. Cooler water, gentler towel-drying, a wide-tooth comb on wet hair and less heat overall. None of this is uniquely Korean — Korean brands simply make the pleasantest versions of it — and consistency beats any single hero product.

No product returns bleached hair to its previous state; the realistic aim is hair that combs, shines and holds a style while you grow it out and trim. Be equally realistic about stacking chemical services, because a perm or a straightening treatment on top of bleach is where most disasters begin, and a stylist who declines is protecting you. Give an honest history of everything done to your hair, box dye and home toners included, since the chemistry depends on it entirely.

hair.title: Postpartum Hair Shedding: What to Expect
hair.h1: Postpartum shedding: common, temporary, and not a product failure
hair.qa: Shedding a few months after childbirth is common and is generally attributed to hair that stayed in its growing phase during pregnancy moving into shedding all at once. It usually settles on its own over the following months. No shampoo prevents it, and if shedding is heavy, prolonged, patchy, or accompanied by other symptoms, that is a conversation for a doctor rather than a shop assistant.

sections.body: During pregnancy a larger share of hair tends to stay in its growing phase instead of shedding on the usual rolling schedule. After birth that synchronisation unwinds and the delayed shedding arrives together, typically a couple of months later, which is why it looks so alarming in the shower. It is less that more hair is being lost overall and more that months of ordinary shedding have been compressed into weeks. It commonly settles over the following months, though the timeline varies considerably.

Korea has a well-developed postpartum care culture, 산후조리 (sanhujori), including dedicated postpartum centres, and a body of traditional advice about staying warm and avoiding cold that historically extended to not washing the hair for weeks. Modern practice is far more relaxed, and there is no reason to leave the scalp uncomfortable; a clean scalp is easier to live with than a neglected one. The genuinely useful part of the tradition is its underlying principle — rest, food and help — which matters more here than any product.

Handle the hair gently: a wide-tooth comb, loose ties rather than tight ponytails, minimal heat and no chemical services while you are already anxious about the mirror. A shorter or layered cut makes shedding less visible and is easier to manage with a baby. Regrowth at the hairline often returns as short wispy pieces that refuse to lie flat for a while — that is the recovery showing, not a new problem. Resist panic-buying an anti-hair-loss line, because this is not what those are for.

See a clinician if shedding is still heavy well beyond the first year, if it is patchy rather than diffuse, if the scalp itself is sore or scaly, or if it comes with fatigue, weight change or feeling cold — iron levels and thyroid function are worth checking and neither is something to guess at. Breastfeeding also affects what any prescribed option can be. This page is general information; the specifics of your own recovery belong in an appointment.

hair.title: Reading Korean Scalp Labels: 두피 Vocabulary
hair.h1: 두피 (dupi): the Korean scalp words printed on the bottle
hair.qa: 두피 (dupi) means scalp, and it is the word that separates Korea's scalp aisle from its hair aisle. Learning a dozen more — 탈모, 비듬, 각질, 진정, 보습, 쿨링, 약산성, 손상모 — is enough to work out what a Korean bottle is for without a translation app. Because much of the wording is regulated, it is more informative than English marketing copy usually is.

sections.body: 두피 (dupi) is scalp and 모발 (mobal) is the hair strand, and a Korean bottle almost always states which of the two it is for. 각질 (gakjil) means dead surface skin — the flakes and buildup a scaling product targets. 피지 (piji) is sebum, 비듬 (bideum) is dandruff, and 탈모 (talmo) is hair loss. Six words cover most of the aisle: a bottle leading with 두피 is scalp care, one leading with 모발 or 손상모 (sonsangmo, damaged hair) is for the lengths.

진정 (jinjeong) is calming and appears on anything aimed at irritation or the look of redness. 보습 (boseup) is moisturising. 쿨링 is exactly what it sounds like and usually means menthol. 볼륨 promises lift, 딥클렌징 a stronger wash, and 스케일링 the exfoliating step before shampoo. 영양 (yeongyang) translates as nourishment and is the one to read sceptically — it is a marketing word rather than a technical one, and tells you only that a product is rich, not what is in it.

약산성 (yaksanseong) means mildly acidic, a real formulation choice that suits scalp and hair better than an alkaline wash. 저자극 (jeojageuk) is low-irritation, and it is a claim rather than a standard. 무실리콘 is silicone-free, 두피 전용 (dupi jeonyong) means scalp-only, and 헤어팩 is a hair mask. One quirk worth knowing: 린스 (rinseu, from 'rinse') is the older Korean word for conditioner, while 트리트먼트 normally signals something richer than an everyday rinse-out.

sections.h: The words that carry legal weight
sections.body: Two labels mean something in regulation rather than in marketing. 기능성화장품 (functional cosmetics) is a defined category with approved purposes and approved wording — including the sentence about helping to relieve hair-loss symptoms, which is why that phrase reads identically across competing brands. 의약외품 (quasi-drug) sits a step above and covers medicated shampoos containing actives such as antifungals. Neither guarantees a product suits you, but both mean the claim was reviewed by someone, which a slogan never is.
